tldr: We propose DemoMimic, a multi-fingered dexterous manipulation method that learns from a single human demonstration. By combining simulation reinforcement learning focused on surface alignment and sustained contact with imitation learning, a single policy can manipulate diverse objects varying in shape, mass, and friction.
hero_caption: Learned from just one human demonstration (top), a single policy successfully performs dexterous manipulation tasks, such as opening boxes and moving bottles, across diverse unseen objects differing in size, material, and friction (bottom).
overview:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered robot hands is one of the grand goals in robotics. However, collecting large amounts of high-quality data via teleoperation remains extremely difficult. Learning from human demonstration data is a promising alternative, but simply retargeting human joint motions to a robot often causes contacts to slip due to differences in hand scale and finger kinematics, leading to failure in the real world.

Recently, sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been used to refine these motions. Yet, existing approaches often overfit to the forgiving contact physics of simulators, resulting in fingers slipping or losing contact when deployed on real hardware (the sim-to-real gap). Furthermore, they struggle to generalize beyond the single object instance used during training.

To overcome this, the authors developed DemoMimic, a framework focusing on the local geometry around contact points. In simulation, it learns robust contacts using an Alignment Reward that aligns surface normals and a Sustained Contact Reward that encourages maintaining contact over time. For real-world deployment, the policy is split hierarchically: a high-level policy predicts a coarse wrist trajectory from an initial RGB image, and a low-level policy fine-tunes fingertip control using local depth from wrist cameras. As long as the local contact geometry is preserved, a single policy can handle objects of varying sizes, masses, and materials.

In real-world evaluations with a bimanual multi-fingered robot hand system, DemoMimic achieved an average success rate of 71% across four challenging tasks and 16 diverse objects. While strong existing baselines suffered severe performance drops in the real world, DemoMimic minimized the sim-to-real gap and demonstrated strong generalization across two different robot hand embodiments.
contributions: Proposed DemoMimic, a multi-fingered dexterous manipulation framework that zero-shot generalizes from a single human demonstration to diverse objects with varying sizes and physical properties.
Designed an Alignment Reward and a Sustained Contact Reward that prevent simulator-specific contact slips and establish stable, sustained contact in the real world.

Constructed a hierarchical policy architecture that decouples global wrist guidance (RGB-guided) from local contact control (wrist-depth-guided), operating without any real-time object pose estimator.
Achieved a 71% success rate across 16 objects and four tasks on real bimanual multi-fingered hands (two hand embodiments), demonstrating significantly better sim-to-real transfer than baselines.

sections.heading: Beyond Parallel Grippers: Multi-Fingered Dexterity and the Sim-to-Real Barrier
sections.summary: Everyday household tasks require dexterity beyond parallel grippers, but collecting teleoperation data for multi-fingered hands is notoriously difficult. While refining human demonstrations via simulation RL is promising, deep challenges remain regarding real-world transfer and generalization to unseen objects.
sections.details:
For robots to use tools or assemble parts like humans, contact-rich dexterous manipulation—impossible with parallel-jaw grippers—is indispensable. However, collecting teleoperation data for multi-fingered hands is extremely hard to scale due to finger occlusions, lack of haptic feedback, and structural mismatches between human and robot hands.

Learning from human demonstrations has therefore emerged as an attractive alternative. Yet, simple geometric retargeting from human to robot causes contacts to fail under slight hand or object mismatches, offering no feedback recovery. Consequently, residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL)—which learns adjustments on top of a reference trajectory in simulation—has gained strong attention.

However, prior works suffer from two major shortcomings in real-world deployment. First, they exploit forgiving contact physics in simulators (e.g., objects not slipping even if contact is momentarily lost), leading to immediate failure on real hardware. Second, they overfit to a single object instance, breaking down when object size or mass changes slightly.

To break through these limitations, the authors propose DemoMimic. Recognizing that local contact geometry is shared across object instances of the same category, DemoMimic combines contact-centric reward design with depth-based hierarchical imitation learning. This enables a single policy to manipulate diverse objects from just one human demonstration.

sections.heading: Evaluating Contact: The Decisive Difference from Prior RL and Imitation Learning
sections.summary: Prior works prioritized tracking object poses while neglecting rewards for contact quality. They also suffered from relying on object pose estimators and lacking instance generalization. DemoMimic addresses these issues with contact-centric rewards and a hierarchical policy.
sections.details:
In human-to-robot RL, the hardest challenge lies in reward design for sim-to-real transfer. Conventional demonstration-guided RL methods (such as ObjDex, DexMachina, and HERMES) have primarily rewarded how closely the robot matches the target object trajectory.

However, they differ sharply in how they treat contact:
- ObjDex: Does not explicitly reward contact.
- DexMachina: Encourages contact in roughly the same regions as the demonstration, but lacks fine control over contact forces.
- HERMES: Employs a coarse design, rewarding only time steps where the number of detected contact points exceeds a threshold.

In contrast, DemoMimic directly rewards precisely aligning robot link normals with object surface normals, as well as sustaining continuous contact force without easing off over a temporal window. While this difference may seem subtle in simulation, it makes a decisive difference in the real world between slipping off and firmly holding contact.

Furthermore, for real-world deployment, prior works often assumed accurate object pose tracking or were confined to a single object size. DemoMimic focuses on local depth from wrist-mounted cameras, removing the need for explicit object pose tracking and absorbing shape and size variations across object instances.

sections.heading: DemoMimic Architecture: From Contact-Centric Residual RL to Hierarchical Imitation Learning
sections.summary: The method consists of two main stages: privileged data generation via residual RL in simulation, and distillation into a hierarchical imitation learning policy. The policy operates solely on real-world RGB-D observations without privileged information.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Residual Reinforcement Learning in Simulation
First, human and object trajectories from a demonstration clip are retargeted to the robot's joint space. Using this trajectory as a baseline, a residual RL policy $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$ learns joint offset adjustments in simulation. Two key contact rewards prevent unrealistic sim behaviors:

- **Alignment Reward (AR)**: Evaluates how well the robot link's surface normal aligns with the object surface normal at the contact point (driving their dot product toward -1). It also evaluates the orientation of links scheduled to make contact in subsequent steps, encouraging smooth contact transitions.
- **Sustained Contact Reward (SCR)**: In time windows where the human maintains contact, rewards are given quadratically based on the continuous streak of steps during which contact force stays above a threshold. While simulation allows flickering contacts to succeed, real-world friction drops immediately cause failure, making the incentive to sustain contact critical.

### 3.2 Imitation Learning Policy Distillation
Because the privileged RL teacher policy relies on true object poses, it is distilled into a student policy operating on real camera observations. The architecture is split into two levels:

- **High-Level Guidance Policy ($\pi_H$)**: A Diffusion Policy that predicts a coarse nominal wrist trajectory from a single initial egocentric RGB image. To bridge the visual sim-to-real gap, it is trained on synthetic photorealistic images generated by NVIDIA's generative model Cosmos-Transfer-2.5.
- **Low-Level Contact Policy ($\pi_L$)**: A Diffusion Policy that takes real-time local depth from both wrist cameras, robot proprioception, and the wrist guidance trajectory from $\pi_H$ to output absolute joint position targets. By focusing on local contact geometry, it remains invariant to global object shape or color.

### 3.3 Real-World Inference
At runtime, $\pi_H$ generates a wrist trajectory from the first egocentric RGB image. During execution, stereo images from wrist cameras are processed into clean depth maps in real time via FoundationStereo, and $\pi_L$ continuously generates joint commands in a closed-loop fashion. No 3D bounding box or object pose tracking is required.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Conquering 16 Objects and Crushing the Sim-to-Real Gap
sections.summary: Using bimanual Franka arms with two types of 5-fingered hands, we evaluated four tasks: Open the box, Lift the lid, Push the box, and Move the bottle. DemoMimic achieved an average success rate of 71% across 16 objects, and contact force analysis revealed why baselines failed in the real world.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The real system features bimanual Franka Research 3 arms equipped with either 15-DoF Tesollo DG-5F hands or 22-DoF Sharpa hands. Four tasks test fingertip positioning and force regulation:
1. **Open the box**: Smoothly opening a box by pressing down on both lid edges with both hands.
2. **Lift the lid**: Hooking fingertips under the lip of an appliance (e.g., a waffle maker) and lifting it open.
3. **Push the box**: Applying both hands to the box flanks to slide it laterally.
4. **Move the bottle**: Firmly grasping a bottle, lifting it, and transporting it to a target location.

Baselines include DexMachina* and HERMES*, along with ablation variants removing specific reward components.

### 4.2 Generalization Across Diverse Objects
Across 16 objects varying significantly in size, weight, material (wood, plastic, metal, cardboard, fabric), and surface friction, DemoMimic achieved an overall average success rate of 71%. It performed consistently across different hand embodiments, reaching 76% on Sharpa and 65% on Tesollo.
The only noticeable drop was on the "Robot Hand Box" in the box opening task (39%). This box had a heavily rounded lid edge, breaking the local contact geometry assumed in the human demonstration. This confirms that as long as local contact geometry is preserved, DemoMimic easily generalizes despite variations in global scale and mass.

### 4.3 Why Do Prior Methods Fail on Hardware?
In simulation, both DexMachina* and HERMES* achieved high success rates (>90%). However, on the real robot, both suffered from high drop rates during box opening and failed heavily.
Real-world contact analysis reveals why (see Figure F6). HERMES* slipped off the intended lid contact points. DexMachina* reached the correct position but lacked sufficient normal force, causing the fingers to lift under hinge resistance. In contrast, DemoMimic maintained strong normal forces on the target surface without slipping, successfully completing the manipulation.

### 4.4 Ablation Analysis
Removing the sustained contact reward (-SCR) caused the drop rate in box opening to jump to nearly 100%. In simulation, momentary contact loss is tolerated without dropping the object, encouraging rapid finger tapping. Removing the alignment reward (-AR) led to severe contact force fluctuations over time, inducing slips in the real world. Only when both rewards are present does the policy produce robust, persistent grasps.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Expanding Robot Dexterity from a Single Human Move
sections.summary: DemoMimic unlocks sim-to-real multi-fingered manipulation across diverse objects from just one human demonstration, powered by contact-centric rewards and local geometry. Current limitations include open-loop high-level planning and restricted workspace coverage.
sections.details:
This work presented DemoMimic, a framework for learning dexterous multi-fingered manipulation from a single human demonstration by leveraging local contact geometry. By incorporating an Alignment Reward (AR) and a Sustained Contact Reward (SCR) in simulation RL and distilling them into a wrist-depth-based local controller, the method achieved zero-shot generalization across objects differing in scale, weight, and material on real robot hardware.

Nevertheless, the authors note several limitations:
1. **Open-Loop High-Level Policy**: Because $\pi_H$ generates the wrist trajectory upfront from a single RGB frame, it cannot adapt if the object moves significantly or the scene changes mid-task. Future work should extend this to a closed-loop planner conditioned on language instructions.
2. **Workspace Constraints**: Although initial object poses were randomized, the effective workspace remains restricted to a desktop area.
3. **Task Scope**: The approach was validated on four tasks, and broader generalizability needs further exploration.
4. **Prerequisite Object Pose Trajectories**: Demonstrations currently require accurate 3D object pose trajectories in addition to human hand tracking. Future research could leverage video foundation models to extract object trajectories directly from in-the-wild human videos.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details — Visual Transfer via Generative AI and Bimanual Hardware
sections.summary: Details on simulation data generation, photorealistic RGB synthesis using Cosmos-Transfer-2.5, and the experimental setup featuring bimanual Franka arms with Tesollo and Sharpa multi-fingered hands.
sections.details:
### A. Demonstration Retargeting and Residual RL Details
Demonstrations were sourced from the ARCTIC dataset and Meta Quest hand tracking. These were retargeted to robot arms and hands using inverse kinematics (Pinocchio). Fingertip keypoints in contact with objects were heavily weighted to preserve contact topology.
The RL action space consists of relative joint angle residuals over the retargeted trajectory, executed via PD control at 60 Hz.

### B. Sim-to-Real Image Synthesis via Cosmos-Transfer-2.5
The high-level guidance policy $\pi_H$ predicts wrist trajectories from real RGB images, but a large visual domain gap exists between simulation and reality. To bridge this, NVIDIA's Cosmos-Transfer-2.5 was used. Feeding in simulation initial RGB images along with prompts like 'a toolbox on a wooden desk' generated photorealistic images with realistic lighting and textures, augmenting the imitation learning dataset.

### C. Hardware Setup and Stereo Processing
The physical setup consists of two 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arms equipped with either 15-DoF Tesollo DG-5F hands or 22-DoF Sharpa hands, totaling up to 54 DoF across both arms and hands.
Each wrist is fitted with a ZED Mini stereo camera running FoundationStereo at 10 Hz to generate low-noise depth images. The low-level policy crops depth within 0.4 m of the wrist, filtering background clutter and focusing exclusively on local contact geometry to output control commands at 30 Hz.

captions.F10: Physical experimental setup: bimanual Franka arms mounted with Tesollo hands (left) or Sharpa hands (right), equipped with a central egocentric RGB camera and stereo depth cameras on each wrist.

takeaways: By focusing on local contact geometry, a single local-depth policy can generalize dexterous manipulation across objects differing in global shape, scale, and mass.

In sim-to-real transfer, combining an Alignment Reward that aligns surface normals with a Sustained Contact Reward that maintains contact streaks effectively counters the forgiving contact physics of simulators.

Decoupling global wrist approach (predicted from RGB) from local fingertip control (closed-loop from wrist depth) provides the key structural robustness needed for complex multi-fingered manipulation.
limitations: The high-level policy predicts wrist trajectories in an open-loop manner from a single initial RGB image, leaving it unable to recover from sudden object shifts or environmental disturbances during execution.
Training requires precise 3D object pose trajectories from the human demonstration, necessitating additional tools before learning directly from arbitrary unconstrained videos.
Generalization fails when the local contact geometry of the object differs significantly from the demonstration, such as lids with heavily rounded edges.
